newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ryanair profits up but trading tough.
newsitem.headline: Ryanair profits up but trading tough.

text.p: Ryanair Holdings Ltd, Ireland's low-cost, no-frills airline which floated on Nasdaq and the Irish Stock Exchange in May, said on Monday it was expanding its fleet and routes despite intense price competition.

"As always in the airline business, trading conditions continue to be tough," chief executive Michael O'Leary said in a results statement. "During the remainder of the year Ryanair will shoulder further challenges ... despite facing continued intense price competition throughout our network."

The group, which reported pre-tax profit up 38 percent at 6.04 million pounds ($8.7 million) for the three months to June 1997 on revenues of 41.32 million, said it planned to increase the size of its fleet by one-third and intended to open up new routes.

Ryanair's May flotation on both New York's Nasdaq and Ireland's ISEQ index, the first Irish company to seek a simultaneous quote in both Ireland and the U.S., was 18 times oversubscribed at a launch price of 195 Irish pence. By 1440 GMT on Monday Ryanair was quoted at 375 pence.

After the Initial Public Offering it said there was a 50-50 split in take-up of stock between the United States and Europe, and 86 percent of Ryanair employees had subscribed for a total of 2.2 million Irish pounds worth of shares.
The flotation price capitalised the airline at 308 million Irish pounds.

Ryanair, which has been operating for 12 years and has a fleet of 15 Boeing 737-200 aircraft, said in Monday's results statement that it had agreed to purchase a further 737 aircraft at a cost of $9.25 million.
The group will take delivery of the 737 and four additional aircraft before the end of the year, by which time the total fleet will have risen to 20 aircraft, it said.

Speculation that the company would seek a listing was ignited after U.S. entrepreneur David Bonderman became Ryanair chairman in December 1996 after taking a 20 percent stake in the airline. Bonderman took over from former GPA chief Tony Ryan whose family founded Ryanair.
Since the flotation Ryanair has opened five new routes, to Brussels, Paris and Stockholm as well as Bristol and Kerry.
It said the average load factor on the three new European routes was currently in excess of 75 percent.

The airline said its balance sheet had benefited from the IPO in May and cash and liquid resources had increased to 61 million Irish pounds in June 1997 from 24 million in March 1997 while long-term debt fell to 2.8 million from 33.7 million. ($ = 0.696 Irish Pounds)
